title: Granite Harbor — data controls & deployment options discovery
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployment tradeoffs
summary: Initial security posture intake focused on key management and access controls. Customer prefers private control of keys but open to dedicated if latency/cost profile fits. Action items: share SOC2 report, KMS integration notes, schedule deep-dive demo and perf run. Customer will circulate retention policy and high-level compliance timeline.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-08
Start: 16:30 PDT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Mike Larkin (CTO), Dana Chen (Head of Security), Rahul Patel (DevOps), Sofia Morales (PM)

Auto-summary (auto-gen): quick intake on KMS and access, leaning to private/dedicated, need SOC2 evidence and perf numbers.

[00:00] Jordan Hayes: hey thanks everyone for making time, i'm jordan from redwood, i'm the account lead for this region, thrilled to chat a bit about your security and deployment constraints.
[00:14] Mike Larkin: hey jordan, yeah thanks, i'll jump in a little. we're trying to figure out how to run inference for our routing assistant and -- big picture we need strong controls. SOC2 is table stakes, also we have strict key ownership rules.
[00:28] Dana Chen: thanks. specifically for us we need customer-managed keys and audit logs that are tamper-evident, plus SSO via our existing adfs/saml provider. any hosted option needs to respect that.
[00:41] Priya Nair: got it, thanks dana. quick clarifying q, when you say customer-managed keys do you mean HSM-backed KMS in your cloud account or on-prem HSM?
[00:50] Dana Chen: ideally HSM in our cloud account (we use GCP KMS currently) — but if we needed on-prem HSM we could consider that too; it's tougher.
[01:03] Rahul Patel: also worth noting our latency SLO is sub-120ms p95 for short prompt generation on core flows, if that's helpful.
[01:12] Jordan Hayes: that's super useful. just to level-set, redwood supports hosted, dedicated reserved pools, and private deployments. for customer-managed keys we have integrations for bring-your-own-kms where you hold keys in your cloud provider and we encrypt model cache and logs with those keys. for on-prem HSM we do a different package — tends to look like private deployment.
[01:35] Sofia Morales: quick question on RBAC — can we map our groups from SAML into admin/editor/viewer roles? we want to restrict model version rollouts to a small team.
[01:45] Priya Nair: yes, we support SSO/SAML with group mapping to RBAC roles, there's also token-level scopes for API keys so you can narrow access to embeddings vs generation endpoints. mapping sometimes needs a small claim transform if you're using custom attributes.
[02:02] Dana Chen: and audit logs — what retention and immutability options do you provide? we have a 7-year retention requirement for some audit trails.
[02:10] Jordan Hayes: good, on audit logging we stream logs to your cloud logging (stackdriver/cloudwatch) or to an S3 bucket. logs are signed server-side for tamper evidence; retention configurable at customer side if you supply the bucket, so you can set lifecycle rules for 7 years. for hosted customers who don't give us a bucket we maintain logs for x days — i'll send the exact matrix.
[02:34] Mike Larkin: can you clarify the difference between dedicated and private again? like if we want your managed infra but keys in our account, which path is that?
[02:44] Priya Nair: so dedicated is reserved GPU pools managed by redwood in our cloud tenancy, you get isolation and reserved capacity, and we can integrate with your KMS via cross-project IAM, but the control plane remains hosted. private deployment is where the control plane sits in your VPC or on-prem — full control, which lets you own keys and meeting your residency constraints more strictly.
[03:06] Rahul Patel: so with dedicated we'd still have vestiges of redwood control plane? is there a split in responsibility like who has the signed logs or who can see token metadata?
[03:15] Jordan Hayes: correct, with dedicated the control plane is still redwood-managed; we can restrict access and provide RBAC so redwood staff can't access customer data — and we provide audit trails for any admin actions. for the strongest separation, private deployment moves the control plane into your environment and you operate the control plane.
[03:33] Dana Chen: another compliance note — do you have SOC2 type II and any ISO certs?
[03:38] Jordan Hayes: yes, SOC2 type II, and we're in process for ISO27001 (timeline Q3). i'll attach the reports after the call.
[03:46] Sofia Morales: mike, on the product side, our worry is friction for devs. if we go private, devs might need a different onboarding. what's the dev experience parity?
[03:56] Priya Nair: parity is a big goal — same API surface and SDKs regardless of hosting. small ops differences: in private you might run a local agent for observability forwarding, but code-level calls look the same.
[04:11] Mike Larkin: okay, good. dana, any blockers for us with respect to encryption at rest for model weights + cache?
[04:18] Dana Chen: we require encryption at rest with keys we control for any customer data and persistent caches. ephemeral caches are okay if they are protected. also need to know what logs contain — no PII in logs.
[04:30] Jordan Hayes: we redact PII by default in logs where possible and can configure stricter redaction rules. model weights are encrypted at rest; kv cache and model artifacts can be encrypted with your KMS if you choose BYOK.
[04:43] Rahul Patel: earlier you mentioned signed logs, can you walk through how replay or tamper detection would work?
[04:49] Priya Nair: broadly: logs are hashed and signed and we provide a hash chain; if you push logs to your storage you can verify the chain. for hosted we keep an integrity record and will share validation proofs on request as part of our security package.
[05:05] Mike Larkin: sounds promising. what about token-level cost visibility or token-level tracing for compliance audits?
[05:11] Jordan Hayes: the console provides token-level breakdowns and per-route traces, you can export traces to your SIEM too. for audit purposes you can pull a timeline of calls filtered by user and model.
[05:24] Dana Chen: ok, let's talk about retention — if a user asks for data deletion, what's the kill-switch?
[05:29] Priya Nair: we support redact/delete APIs tied to request ids; for private deployments you control the underlying storage so deletion is immediate according to your policies. for hosted/dedicated we follow your del policies and will delete data and remove it from backups per SLA windows — i'll include the retention/deletion SLA in the doc i send.
[05:50] Sofia Morales: on a related note, we do long-term analytics of embeddings and want to avoid accidental exposure of those vectors. are embeddings treated as PII or do you treat them differently?
[05:59] Jordan Hayes: embeddings are treated as user data; retention and access controls apply. you can opt to not store embeddings in persistent storage and only keep ephemeral caches, or store them encrypted in your bucket under your key.
[06:16] Mike Larkin: any limitations on SAML providers? we use ADFS currently and we have a few custom claims.
[06:23] Priya Nair: ADFS and Okta, Azure AD are all supported; custom claims usually require a small mapping step. if you have SAML metadata we can import it, and we support signed assertions and attribute-level mapping.
[06:37] Rahul Patel: let's switch to perf a bit — Priya, is there a recommended instance type for low-latency LLM inference? we currently run a 13b internally but want managed service.
[06:46] Priya Nair: for sub-120ms p95 you'll likely want a lower-latency GPU (A100 or equivalent) with tuned kernels + quantized model variants. Dedicated pools let you pick instance shapes and model quantization; private gives even more control over kernel and compiler flags. we'll propose config options in the perf sheet.
[07:05] Mike Larkin: and the cost tradeoff, roughly how much more does that cost versus a generic hosted instance?
[07:11] Jordan Hayes: broad ballpark: dedicated/reserved tends to be 30-40% more than basic hosted per token but gives you predictable throughput and lower tail latency; private deployments add ops overhead but can be optimized for cost per inference depending on scale. i'll include ballpark numbers in the follow-up.
[07:31] Dana Chen: we have a regulatory constraint: some data must not leave EU regions. can Redwood be deployed to meet region residency?
[07:39] Priya Nair: yes, we have region-specific deployments and can limit routing to EU-only. private and dedicated deployments in region are common for that use case.
[07:50] Sofia Morales: can we get a proof-of-concept where we run a small sandbox connected to our KMS and a sample dataset?
[07:59] Jordan Hayes: absolutely. typical POC flow: 1) sign an NDA/POC agreement, 2) you give perf targets and a test dataset, 3) we spin up a dedicated pool or private sandbox and integrate your KMS, 4) run perf and security checks and produce a report.
[08:17] Mike Larkin: timeline — we want to decide in ~6 weeks, with pilot in 8. is that feasible?
[08:23] Jordan Hayes: yes; tight but doable. we'll need your retention policy and volume estimates to size the pilot.
[08:29] Dana Chen: last security nit — SSO logout and session revocation needs to be quick if an account is deprovisioned.
[08:36] Priya Nain: (mispronounced) — priya here — we support session revocation via our auth provider hooks and can honor immediate token revocation for SAML users; for API keys we can revoke centrally and it takes effect immediately.
[08:52] Rahul Patel: one more ops question: how do you handle model updates/rollouts? we need staged rollouts and quick rollback capability.
[08:59] Jordan Hayes: our rollout system supports canary and A/B rollouts with automatic fallback on error rates. you can pin model versions per route and schedule rollouts.
[09:10] Mike Larkin: good. i'm trying to think of anything else — maybe legal around data processing agreements?
[09:16] Jordan Hayes: we have a standard DPA and can incorporate specific clauses for data residency and subprocessor disclosures; i'll share the template.
[09:24] (pause / cross-talk)
[09:36] Sofia Morales: thanks, this has been really helpful — dana, rahul, any remaining blockers?
[09:42] Dana Chen: from security side, main items: SOC2 evidence, BYOK integration details, audit log immutability verification, and retention SLA. after we see docs we'll schedule a deeper technical call.
[09:55] Rahul Patel: dev side needs perf numbers and an integration runbook.
[10:02] Jordan Hayes: perfect. quick recap and next steps — i'll email SOC2/ISO notes, priya will send perf spreadsheet and propose demo slots, dana will share retention policy. we'll aim to have POC kickoff window within 2 weeks after docs are exchanged.
[10:20] Mike Larkin: sounds good. one last small question — do you support customer-managed secrets in HSM for model signing/verify?
[10:28] Priya Nair: yes, in private deployments you can bring HSM for signing keys; in dedicated we have options to integrate to your cloud HSM for key wrapping. i'll outline the options.
[10:40] Jordan Hayes: okay, if there's nothing else we'll wrap. thanks everyone for the time.
[10:47] Dana Chen: thanks, appreciate it.
[10:50] Sofia Morales: thanks all.
[10:52] End of recording.
